before.name: Dugong
before.habitat: Coastal seas, estuaries and seagrass beds
before.rarity: Rarely seen in Singapore waters; no population estimate implied
before.summary: A marine mammal that grazes on seagrass. Singapore records link this quiet swimmer to shallow coastal waters and river mouths.
before.identification: A bulky grey-brown body, blunt bristled muzzle, paired front flippers and a fluked tail. It has no dorsal fin.
before.diet: Mainly seagrass, gathered from underwater meadows.
before.activity: Feeding and resting alternate; the local NParks account describes night feeding and daytime rest in deeper water.
before.behaviour: May travel alone, with another dugong or in small groups. It surfaces to breathe and remains fully aquatic.
before.reproduction: A female normally produces one calf after a pregnancy lasting about thirteen to fourteen months. She nurses the calf. These general life-history notes do not establish a Singapore breeding season.
before.singapore: NParks records it mainly from the north-eastern Johor Straits. Records also include Changi, Pulau Ubin, Pulau Tekong and Labrador. A recorded location does not guarantee a sighting.
before.ecologicalRole: Seagrass feeding connects coastal vegetation with the marine food web.
before.pressures: Boat propellers, fishing-net entanglement, water pollution and loss of seagrass feeding grounds threaten dugongs.
before.watch: Observe from shore where possible. Never chase, feed or approach an animal with a boat. Report a stranded animal to NParks or ACRES and follow their instructions.
before.fact: A dugong has no dorsal fin.

before.name: Equatorial spitting cobra
before.habitat: Scrub, forest edges and suburban greenery
before.fact: A hood and hiss are defensive warnings, not an invitation to move closer.
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.summary: A venomous native snake that sometimes enters built areas. Learning about it should build respect and safe distance, never encourage approaching or handling.
before.identification: Often glossy black locally, with a broad head and an expandable hood. A snake does not need to raise its hood to be dangerous.
before.diet: Small animals, including rats and toads.
before.activity: Often diurnal, though an encounter is possible at other times.
before.behaviour: May raise the forebody, spread the hood and hiss when threatened. It can also spray venom defensively toward an attacker’s eyes.
before.reproduction: An egg-laying snake. Do not disturb hidden snakes, egg sites or shelter; young snakes must also be left alone.
before.singapore: NParks describes it as common in scrub and suburban habitats. Its secretive nature means encounter frequency and national threat status are different measures.
before.ecologicalRole: A predator of small vertebrates in terrestrial food webs.
before.pressures: Killing through fear and conflict with people can harm native snakes.
before.watch: Back away and keep others and pets away. Never try to catch it; seek urgent medical help for a bite or venom exposure.

funFacts.title: A warning display
funFacts.text: A hood and hiss are defensive warnings, not an invitation to move closer.

funFacts.title: A useful hunter
funFacts.text: Rats and toads are among this cobra’s natural prey.

before.name: Estuarine crocodile
before.habitat: Estuaries, mangroves and former prawn ponds
before.fact: It often basks by day and hunts mainly at night.
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2021
before.summary: A large native reptile of estuaries and wetlands. Crocodiles can be difficult to detect in water; viewing must be from designated safe areas.
before.identification: Broad snout, armoured body and a muscular, flattened tail. Only the eyes and nostrils may show above the surface.
before.diet: Fish and other animals; also scavenges.
before.activity: Often basks by day and hunts mainly at night.
before.behaviour: Spends time concealed in water or vegetation. Adults may use freshwater as well as saline habitats despite the name ‘saltwater crocodile’.
before.reproduction: The female lays eggs in a vegetation nest and guards it. A concealed nest area must never be approached.
before.singapore: Recorded from northern wetlands and estuaries, including Sungei Buloh. Records are not an invitation to approach water edges outside permitted areas.
before.ecologicalRole: A large wetland predator and scavenger.
before.pressures: Loss of estuarine habitat and conflict with people. Keeping safe separation protects visitors and wildlife.
before.watch: Follow park warnings and stay on designated paths. Keep well away from water edges, do not feed, and alert park staff to unsafe encounters.

funFacts.title: Not just salt water
funFacts.text: Despite one of its names, it also uses freshwater habitats.

before.name: Four-lined tree frog
before.habitat: Trees and shrubs near breeding water
before.rarity: Common in suburban and disturbed habitats
before.fact: Its eggs begin life inside foam above water; the tadpoles later drop into the water.
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.summary: A climbing frog of trees, shrubs and gardens. It uses vegetation for hunting and puts its eggs in foam above water rather than laying an exposed mass in a pond.
before.identification: Slender limbs, a pointed snout and expanded toe pads. Four dark back stripes are common, but some individuals are spotted or less clearly marked.
before.diet: Insects and other small invertebrates.
before.activity: Nocturnal.
before.behaviour: Climbs vegetation with its toe pads. Calling can reveal animals that blend into leaves and bark.
before.reproduction: Builds a foam nest over water. After hatching, tadpoles drop into the water and continue development there.
before.singapore: A common native frog of suburban and rural greenery, as well as disturbed forest. It is nationally Least Concern in RDB3.
before.ecologicalRole: An insect predator above ground, with an aquatic tadpole stage linking land and water.
before.pressures: Loss of vegetation and breeding water, disturbance and chemical pollution can reduce suitable habitat.
before.watch: Do not peel open foam nests, collect tadpoles or handle the frogs. Watch from the path.

before.name: Great-billed heron
before.rarity: Uncommon resident restricted to coastal habitat
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · assessed 2024
before.fact: This heron reaches roughly 1.15 metres in length—a striking contrast with Singapore's tiny kingfishers.
before.globalAssessmentNote: Assessment date and category verified through the IUCN SSC Heron Specialist Group’s Red List table (version 2024-2).
before.summary: A very large coastal heron with an imposing bill. Singapore's population has a Critically Endangered national assessment even though the species has a much wider international range.
before.identification: An adult is mostly dusky grey, with a long neck and unusually heavy, dark pointed bill. Breeding birds develop elongated plumes. Young birds are warmer brown and more streaked. Bird Society of Singapore gives a length of about 114–115 cm.
before.diet: Fish, crustaceans and other aquatic invertebrates.
before.activity: Can be watched feeding at the shoreline by day. The sources used here do not establish an exclusively daytime activity cycle.
before.behaviour: Usually feeds alone, waiting at the water's edge or moving slowly through the shallows before striking at prey.
before.reproduction: NParks describes nesting in isolated mangrove stands. Protecting suitable nesting trees matters; this guide withholds precise breeding locations and gives no unverified local clutch size.
before.singapore: Occurs in coastal settings, including mangroves, estuaries and offshore islands. Its association with specialised coastal habitat makes everyday inland sightings unlikely; a record at one shoreline is not a population estimate.
before.ecologicalRole: Its prey connects intertidal and shallow-water animals to the coastal bird food web.
before.pressures: NParks identifies loss or disturbance of suitable coastal feeding and nesting areas as conservation concerns. Old population estimates in the legacy profile are not presented as current counts.
before.watch: Use coastal hides and public paths. Stay off restricted islands and mangrove nesting areas. Give a feeding bird space instead of following it along the waterline.

before.name: Greater mousedeer
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.fact: The decisive 2008 rediscovery photographs showed the throat and chest markings needed to identify the species.
before.summary: A small hoofed forest browser with a rounded body and very slender legs. Its rediscovery on Pulau Ubin shows why an animal missing from casual sightings is not necessarily gone.
before.identification: Reddish-brown fur, pale underparts and contrasting throat markings. More robust than the lesser mousedeer; useful photographs show the neck and chest, not just apparent size. It has no antlers.
before.diet: Fallen fruit, tender leaves and other low-growing plant material.
before.activity: Mostly nocturnal; usually feeds quietly on the forest floor.
before.behaviour: Typically encountered alone while browsing or resting under cover. A published Singapore survey also recorded more than one animal together, so solitary does not mean never seen with another.
before.reproduction: Usually produces one well-developed young. Regional accounts describe a pregnancy of roughly five months; this is not a prediction of Singapore birth dates. Juveniles were documented during the Ubin rediscovery study.
before.singapore: Confirmed on Pulau Ubin in 2008 after a long gap in verified records. NParks still includes the species in its 2025 Ubin conservation work. Its limited Singapore distribution does not mean every suitable mainland forest contains it.
before.ecologicalRole: A forest-floor plant consumer and part of the food web linking vegetation to predators.
before.pressures: Habitat disturbance and fragmentation can affect its restricted local habitat. Hunting is a pressure across its wider range. Protecting forest cover and limiting disturbance support its persistence.
before.watch: Keep to permitted paths, observe quietly and never feed or pursue it. Leave dense undergrowth undisturbed and do not share exact resting locations.

funFacts.text: The decisive 2008 rediscovery photographs showed the throat and chest markings needed to identify the species.

funFacts.title: Tiny hooves, no antlers
funFacts.text: Despite the name, a mousedeer is a chevrotain. Males have enlarged canine teeth rather than antlers.

before.name: Green turtle
before.habitat: Shallow coastal water, reefs and seagrass beds
before.fact: Paddle-shaped limbs power long-distance swimming.
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2025
before.summary: A marine turtle that uses tropical and subtropical seas. Adults often graze shallow feeding grounds, while nesting requires accessible sandy beaches.
before.identification: An oval shell with non-overlapping scutes, paddle-like flippers and one pair of scales between the eyes. The shell is usually brownish, not bright green.
before.diet: Adults mainly eat seagrasses and algae; diet changes with life stage.
before.activity: Lives at sea and surfaces for air; nesting is mainly nocturnal.
before.behaviour: Moves between feeding grounds and nesting areas. Its strong front flippers provide propulsion in the water.

before.name: Horsfield’s flying squirrel
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.fact: Its gliding membrane stretches between all four limbs; the long tail is flattened rather than round and bushy.
before.summary: A nocturnal squirrel that glides between trees on a membrane joining its limbs. Its quiet life above the ground makes it much less conspicuous than the daytime squirrels in parks.
before.identification: Dark brown upperparts, a paler orange-buff or whitish underside and rusty edges to the gliding membrane. A rounded head, large eyes and long, flattened, feather-like tail complete its outline.
before.diet: Mainly fruit, with insects also listed in the NParks species account.
before.activity: Active at night; rests in a tree cavity by day.
before.behaviour: Climbs using sharp claws and spreads its membrane to glide. It depends on trees for feeding, shelter and travel. Detailed social behaviour remains poorly studied.
before.reproduction: Gives birth to live young, but the reviewed species account does not establish its mating system, breeding season or litter size. Values from larger flying squirrels are not substituted.
before.singapore: Recorded in Singapore's central forest reserves and in a wooded nature park outside them. Local records require careful identification; difficulty seeing a nocturnal animal is not a population estimate.
before.ecologicalRole: A canopy fruit consumer that also eats small invertebrates. Its precise contribution to seed dispersal in Singapore has not been quantified in the reviewed sources.
before.pressures: Loss of forest and suitable cavity-bearing trees removes shelter and foraging areas. Maintaining connected wooded habitat is important for a species that travels between trees.
before.watch: Observe from permitted routes and avoid flash, sustained spotlighting or disturbance of tree holes. Never lure an animal with food or enter closed areas to seek it.

before.name: House crow
before.habitat: Urban areas, parks and coastal greenery
before.fact: The house crow is not entirely black: look for its greyer neck and chest.
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2018
before.summary: An adaptable crow commonly seen around Singapore’s built areas. It originated in the Indian subcontinent and is an introduced resident here.
before.identification: A black head and wings contrast with a greyer neck and breast. The grey collar is a better starting clue than simply calling any black bird a crow.
before.diet: A wide range of food, including invertebrates, fruit, carrion and accessible food waste.
before.activity: Diurnal.
before.behaviour: Forages opportunistically and can gather around reliable food. Breeding adults may defend the area around their nest or young.
before.reproduction: An egg-laying bird that builds a nest and raises chicks. Defensive swooping can be associated with breeding and does not mean the bird is hunting people.
before.singapore: Common in urban environments and also uses coastal and mangrove settings. It is listed as introduced and nationally Not Applicable.
before.ecologicalRole: A scavenger and omnivore, with possible effects on other birds’ eggs and young.
before.pressures: Food waste and close nesting beside people can lead to conflict.
before.watch: Avoid a defended nesting area and do not feed. Report persistent attacks through the current AVS guidance page.

before.sourceName: Ocean Park Conservation Foundation Hong Kong
before.summary: A coastal dolphin recorded in Singapore waters. Its common pink-dolphin name does not mean every individual is pink.
before.identification: A long narrow beak and a dorsal fin on a raised back area. Colour varies with age and region; grey markings may remain on pale adults.
before.diet: Small fish captured in coastal waters.
before.activity: Surfaces regularly to breathe between dives; Singapore-specific daily activity patterns are not established here.
before.behaviour: A social, fully aquatic mammal. Surface behaviour can include leaps and raising the head above water.
before.reproduction: Females give birth to calves. Hong Kong research reports a pregnancy of about eleven months. Its seasonal calving pattern must not be treated as a Singapore breeding calendar.
before.singapore: NParks includes this dolphin in Singapore's marine mammal list. Its St John's Island trail factsheet documents sightings around the southern islands. This is wild occurrence, not a captive attraction record.
before.ecologicalRole: A predator of coastal fish and part of the marine food web.
before.pressures: Fishing gear, vessel strikes, pollution and coastal habitat disturbance are recognised threats across its range.
before.watch: Do not follow, encircle or feed dolphins. Give them space to travel. Report strandings through local wildlife authorities.
before.fact: Colour changes with age and differs between regions.

before.reproduction: Nests in cavities, including suitable openings in buildings. Urban structures can provide many possible nest sites.

before.pressures: Abundant food waste supports concentrations near homes. National non-native status is separate from its conservation position in its native range.
before.watch: Dispose of food properly and do not feed. Leave active nests and roosting birds undisturbed.

before.activity: Nocturnal.

before.watch: Do not handle a bat or disturb a roost. Observe from a distance and seek professional help for an injured animal.

before.name: Little egret
before.habitat: Rivers, canals, ponds and coastal wetlands
before.rarity: Common migrant; abundance varies with season and site
before.summary: A small white heron that feeds in shallow water. It uses both urban waterways and natural coastal wetlands.
before.identification: White plumage, a slender dark bill, dark legs and yellow feet in typical adults. Young birds can have greener legs.
before.diet: Small fish, crustaceans and insects. Fish and insects are prey here, not added catalogue groups.
before.activity: Often seen feeding in daylight; feeding opportunities depend on water levels.
before.behaviour: May disturb the water with its feet to reveal prey. It can feed with other egrets.
before.reproduction: Builds nests and lays eggs, often in colonies with other waterbirds. Both parents contribute to care. These species-level notes do not claim a local breeding colony.
before.singapore: A familiar migrant at Sungei Buloh and other wetlands, including pond and canal edges. NParks records it throughout the year, with higher numbers commonly between November and January.
before.ecologicalRole: A shallow-water predator that connects small aquatic animals to the wetland food web.
before.pressures: Wetland disturbance and loss can remove feeding and resting places. A locally common visitor still depends on suitable habitat elsewhere along its migration route.
before.watch: Watch from paths or hides. Avoid making birds fly away from feeding or resting areas, and never feed them.
before.fact: Its yellow feet can stir hidden prey from shallow water.

before.name: Long-tailed macaque
before.fact: Its tail can rival the combined length of its head and body.
before.globalStatus: Endangered · 2025
before.summary: Singapore’s familiar forest-edge monkey is a social, adaptable native primate. Food left accessible by people can draw groups into close contact with visitors and homes.
before.identification: Brown-grey coat, relatively pale underside and a tail that can be as long as the head and body together. It differs from the dark, pale-banded langur.
before.diet: Fruit and other plant food, plus insects and other small animals.
before.activity: Mainly diurnal.
before.behaviour: Lives in groups organised around related females. It forages both in trees and on the ground and uses calls, expressions and grooming socially.
before.reproduction: Usually gives birth to one infant. Mothers carry and nurse young, which remain within the social group as they grow.
before.singapore: Commonly encountered in and around forest reserves and some parkland. Feeding changes natural foraging behaviour and increases conflict.
before.ecologicalRole: An omnivore and fruit consumer in forest food webs.
before.pressures: Food-conditioned behaviour, unsafe interactions and habitat fragmentation can create local problems, even for a nationally Least Concern species.
before.watch: Keep food out of sight, secure bags and give the group space. Do not stare, feed, tease or try to touch a monkey.

before.name: Malayan horned frog
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.fact: Its angular outline and brown colouring help a motionless frog disappear among fallen leaves.
before.summary: A leaf-shaped ambush hunter from Singapore's mature forests. Its camouflage is so effective that a call may reveal a frog that the eye has missed.
before.identification: Broad angular head, pointed eyelid projections and a leaf-like snout and brown body. Females are larger than males. Projection length varies, so it should not be the only identification feature.
before.diet: Animal prey on the forest floor, including invertebrates and small vertebrates such as other frogs or lizards.
before.activity: Secretive; calls can be heard around dusk and were recorded during late-afternoon breeding observations in Singapore.
before.behaviour: Remains still in leaf litter and ambushes passing prey. Local researchers have often detected it by its distinctive loud call near streams.
before.reproduction: Breeds in forest streams. A Singapore field study recorded mating and a cluster of gelatinous eggs attached beneath partly submerged bark; larvae develop in water.
before.singapore: Associated with patches of mature forest in the Central Nature Reserves. It is nationally Critically Endangered in RDB3; this guide avoids breeding-site directions.
before.ecologicalRole: An ambush predator that connects leaf-litter prey with larger forest predators; its aquatic young also depend on stream habitat.
before.pressures: Loss or damage to moist forest and stream habitat is a concern, alongside collection for the pet trade across its range.
before.watch: Listen from open trails during permitted hours. Do not use call playback, move leaf litter, enter breeding streams or handle frogs and eggs.

before.name: Malayan porcupine
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.fact: Porcupines cannot shoot their quills. A quill can detach after contact, which helps explain the familiar myth.
before.summary: A large ground-dwelling rodent with striking defensive quills. Camera traps helped establish that this secretive native mammal still survived in Singapore after decades with few reports.
before.identification: A blunt muzzle, stout body, short legs and a short tail. The longest back quills are strongly patterned in black and white. It is a porcupine, not a hedgehog.
before.diet: Fruit, roots and stems, gathered while foraging on the ground.
before.activity: Nocturnal; normally shelters in burrows during daylight.
before.behaviour: Digs burrows and travels on land. A threatened animal can raise its quills, rattle its tail and back towards a threat; leave it room to retreat.
before.reproduction: Gives birth to live young. The Singapore field sources reviewed here do not establish a local breeding season or typical litter size, so no exact reproductive timetable is claimed.
before.singapore: Rediscovered on an offshore island in 2005. Later camera-trap records documented animals in mainland forest reserves and other wooded areas. RDB3 continues to recognise a native, nationally Critically Endangered population.
before.ecologicalRole: Its plant feeding links roots, stems and fallen fruit to the forest food web; burrowing also disturbs small patches of soil.
before.pressures: Forest loss and fragmentation reduce habitat. Hunting for meat and trade in body parts are documented regional pressures; the reviewed sources do not provide a current Singapore hunting rate.
before.watch: Keep a generous distance and never block its path or approach a burrow. Do not attempt to handle an animal or remove its quills.

before.name: Oriental pied hornbill
before.habitat: Parks and wooded areas with fruiting trees
before.fact: A nesting female stays inside a mostly sealed tree cavity while the male brings food.
before.rarity: Recovered; often visible at suitable sites
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2020
before.summary: A conspicuous black-and-white bird with a pale bill and a raised casque. Its return to Singapore is a conservation story linked to suitable habitat and nesting places.
before.identification: Large pale bill, casque above the bill, black wings and upperparts, and a white belly. Look at several features rather than comparing it with a toucan.
before.diet: Mainly fruit, supplemented by small animals.
before.activity: Diurnal; calls and travels through wooded areas.
before.behaviour: Visits fruiting trees and may travel in pairs or groups. Tree cavities are essential for its unusual nesting routine.
before.reproduction: The female and chicks stay in a mostly sealed cavity. The male brings food through a narrow opening.
before.singapore: Now found in suitable parks and wooded areas, including Pulau Ubin. Recovery does not make every site suitable for nesting.
before.ecologicalRole: Fruit consumption can move seeds between patches of vegetation.
before.pressures: Loss of large cavity-bearing trees and disturbance at nests. Nest boxes have supported local conservation efforts.
before.watch: Leave fruit for wildlife. Do not feed, crowd or approach a nesting cavity.

after.name: Oriental pied hornbill
after.habitat: Parks and wooded areas with fruiting trees
after.fact: A nesting female stays inside a mostly sealed tree cavity while the male brings food.
after.rarity: Recovered; often visible at suitable sites
after.summary: A conspicuous black-and-white bird with a pale bill and a raised casque. Its return to Singapore is a conservation story linked to suitable habitat and nesting places.
after.identification: Large pale bill, casque above the bill, black wings and upperparts, and a white belly. Look at several features rather than comparing it with a toucan.
after.diet: Mainly fruit, supplemented by small animals.
after.activity: Moves through wooded areas and the tree canopy, giving loud cackling calls.
after.behaviour: Visits fruiting trees and may travel in pairs or groups. Tree cavities are essential for its unusual nesting routine.
after.reproduction: The female and chicks stay in a mostly sealed cavity. The male brings food through a narrow opening.
after.singapore: Now found in suitable parks and wooded areas, including Pulau Ubin. Recovery does not make every site suitable for nesting.
after.ecologicalRole: Fruit consumption can move seeds between patches of vegetation.
after.pressures: Loss of large cavity-bearing trees and disturbance at nests. Nest boxes have supported local conservation efforts.
after.watch: Leave fruit for wildlife. Do not feed, crowd or approach a nesting cavity.

funFacts.title: Room service in a tree
funFacts.text: The male delivers meals through the small entrance of the sealed nest.

before.name: Plantain squirrel
before.habitat: Trees in forests, parks and gardens
before.fact: Listen for loud chirps and chatter while squirrels move among branches.
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.summary: A familiar squirrel of Singapore’s trees and gardens. It spends daylight hours searching for food and moving quickly between trunks and branches.
before.identification: A bushy tail and a pale stripe above a darker stripe on each flank are useful clues. Check side markings, rather than relying on coat colour alone.
before.diet: Fruit, seeds and other plant food, with some animal food.
before.activity: Diurnal.
before.behaviour: Uses claws to climb and makes quick leaps between branches. Chirps and chatter are part of its communication.
before.reproduction: Young are born in a sheltered nest and depend on their mother. Leave leafy nests undisturbed even when they appear empty.
before.singapore: NParks describes it as the most common squirrel in local urban parks and gardens. It also uses forest and other wooded habitats.
before.ecologicalRole: A seed and fruit consumer within tree-based food webs.
before.pressures: Loss of tree connections and feeding by people can affect normal movement and foraging.
before.watch: Enjoy it from the path. Do not bait it for a photograph or offer snacks.

before.name: Red-cheeked flying squirrel
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.fact: Its broad, flattened tail gives the group its 'arrow-tailed flying squirrel' nickname.
before.summary: A tiny forest squirrel with warm-coloured cheeks and a broad gliding membrane. It is one of Singapore's least conspicuous mammals and needs careful observation to separate it from other gliders.
before.identification: Grey-brown upperparts with rusty colouring, a pale underside, orange-brown cheeks and a flattened tail. NParks describes a narrow white edge along the side of the gliding membrane.
before.diet: Regional observations describe fruit, flowers and leaves, with some insects.
before.activity: Nocturnal and mainly active in trees.
before.behaviour: Glides between trees and shelters in cavities in tall trunks. It appears largely solitary, but detailed social studies are limited.
before.reproduction: Uses sheltered tree holes. Reliable species-specific breeding dates and litter sizes were not established in this review. Frequently repeated numbers in one educational account are actually attributed to a different Hylopetes species.
before.singapore: Recorded from Bukit Timah and Central Catchment forests. The latter records were published in 2013, so the older statement that it occurs only in Bukit Timah is not retained.
before.ecologicalRole: Connects canopy plant resources and small invertebrates with the forest food web. No measured Singapore seed-dispersal rate is claimed.
before.pressures: Loss or degradation of mature forest can remove both food and cavity shelters. Its restricted habitat and small size also make monitoring difficult.
before.watch: Watch quietly from open trails without flash or prolonged direct light. Do not inspect occupied tree cavities or publish exact shelter locations.

before.name: Red junglefowl
before.habitat: Forest edges, scrub and wooded parks
before.rarity: Often seen; domestic hybrids complicate identification
before.fact: Despite feeding on the ground, junglefowl roost in trees.
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2024
before.summary: The wild relative of domestic chickens. Singapore also has free-ranging domestic and hybrid chickens, so every rooster in a park must not be labelled a pure red junglefowl.
before.identification: Males have orange-red neck feathers, dark glossy tails and a red comb. Females are mottled brown. Domestic ancestry cannot be ruled out from one visible trait.
before.diet: Seeds, roots and small invertebrates found on the ground.
before.activity: Diurnal; roosts in trees at night.
before.behaviour: Scratches and pecks through ground cover. Groups have social relationships, with males displaying and crowing.
before.reproduction: Females lay eggs in a ground nest and care for chicks. The young can follow the mother and feed themselves soon after hatching.
before.singapore: Native wild birds and admixed free-ranging birds occur locally. The national Near Threatened assessment applies to the wild species, not all domestic chickens.
before.ecologicalRole: A ground-foraging omnivore that eats seeds and small animals.
before.pressures: Hybridisation with domestic chickens, trapping and loss of suitable habitat.
before.watch: Do not feed or chase. Give hens with chicks room to move and leave ground nests alone.

before.name: Reticulated python
before.fact: ‘Reticulated’ describes the net-like pattern running along its body.
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2018
before.summary: A large native snake with a network-like pattern. It is non-venomous but powerful, and should always be observed without handling or cornering it.
before.identification: Tan or yellow-brown ground colour crossed by dark geometric lines and pale side patches. Its shape and pattern differ from a uniformly dark cobra.
before.diet: Mammals, including rodents; larger individuals can take larger prey.
before.activity: Often nocturnal or hidden during daylight.
before.behaviour: Ambushes prey, constricts it and swallows it whole. It is mainly terrestrial but can climb well.
before.reproduction: Lays eggs; the female coils around the clutch during incubation. Eggs and resting snakes must not be moved by visitors.
before.singapore: A native resident using natural and urban habitats. A drain or green corridor can provide cover, so sightings are not limited to forests.
before.ecologicalRole: A predator of rodents and other mammals.
before.pressures: Road collisions, persecution and conflict in built environments.
before.watch: Keep people and pets away and allow an escape route. Contact a wildlife professional if it is trapped or inside a building.

before.name: Small-toothed palm civet
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.fact: A published Singapore record describes two civets resting against each other in the canopy; the observers could not confirm their relationship.
before.summary: A canopy-dwelling civet that is much less often seen than Singapore's familiar Sumatran palm civet. Published observations of adults and apparent young show how much remains to learn about its forest life.
before.identification: Usually brownish-grey with a darker face and tail, pale forehead marking and three dark lines along the back. Markings vary, so a quick glimpse is insufficient to identify an unfamiliar civet confidently.
before.diet: Fruit is important, alongside insects and small vertebrates. It belongs to the carnivore order but has an omnivorous diet.
before.activity: Nocturnal and strongly arboreal; often rests high in vegetation.
before.behaviour: Often described as solitary. Singapore observers have also recorded pairs resting close together, although their ages and relationship could not always be confirmed.
before.reproduction: Females produce and nurse dependent young. Published Singapore sightings include an apparent juvenile, but those observations do not establish a breeding season or confirm that every pair is a mother and offspring.
before.singapore: Associated with the central nature reserves. A 2023 NUS biodiversity record documents observations in secondary forest during 2022–2023. Exact resting trees are omitted from this guide.
before.ecologicalRole: A fruit eater and predator of small animals. Seed transport is a plausible ecological contribution, but the profile does not claim a measured local dispersal rate or a demonstrated keystone role.
before.pressures: Forest loss and degradation affect canopy habitat. The reviewed literature describes hunting and capture elsewhere in its range; it does not quantify current Singapore exploitation.
before.watch: Use binoculars from permitted paths and leave resting animals undisturbed. Never bait, feed, touch or follow a civet into the forest.

before.name: Spiny hill turtle
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.fact: Its dramatic juvenile shell edges become much less spiky as the turtle grows.
before.summary: A forest-floor turtle with an especially striking shell when young. Singapore's remaining mature forests shelter this locally Endangered reptile.
before.identification: Brown shell with a raised middle ridge and jagged rear edge; dark head and limbs, with reddish marks beside the head. Young turtles have much sharper shell-edge projections than adults.
before.diet: An omnivore. Regional research records fruit and other plant material, some animal food and mushrooms; the proportions in Singapore have not been measured here.
before.activity: NParks describes mainly nocturnal activity; this is not a rule that excludes daytime encounters.
before.behaviour: Adults spend much of their time on land. Younger turtles use water more extensively, so forest-floor and stream habitats both matter.
before.reproduction: Lays eggs. Breeding has been achieved in conservation collections; no Singapore nesting month or clutch-size claim is made here.
before.singapore: Native populations are associated with the Central Nature Reserves. The national assessment is Endangered in RDB3; encounter locations and resting sites are not mapped here.
before.ecologicalRole: Consumes material from several parts of the forest food web. Mushroom eating is documented, but effective fungal-spore dispersal by this species remains a research question.
before.pressures: Forest degradation and collection for trade threaten it. Protecting habitat and preventing collection are central conservation needs.
before.watch: Keep to open paths, leave it where it is and avoid handling or flash. Do not disclose a precise location or collect an animal for a pet.

before.name: Straw-headed bulbul

before.fact: Its loud song has made it a target of the illegal songbird trade.

before.summary: A large songbird whose voice often gives it away before its body appears. Singapore is important to its survival, while capture for the songbird trade has damaged populations elsewhere.
before.identification: A straw-coloured crown, dark facial stripes and pale streaks on the breast. It is larger than many familiar urban bulbuls.
before.diet: Fruit, berries and insects.
before.activity: Diurnal; often heard from dense vegetation.
before.behaviour: Forages in thick foliage near water and forest edges. Its loud, bubbling song is a useful clue, but listening must not become playback or disturbance.
before.reproduction: An egg-laying bird whose nesting cover needs protection. Do not seek nests or publish nest locations; local timing is not predicted by this guide.
before.singapore: Found in suitable wooded habitats, including Pulau Ubin. Local occurrence and its global Critically Endangered label refer to different geographic scales.
before.ecologicalRole: A fruit-eater and insect predator within wooded habitats.
before.pressures: Illegal capture for the songbird trade and habitat loss. Singapore’s species action plan includes habitat work and protection against poaching.
before.watch: Listen quietly from paths. Never play calls to draw it out, set up bait or publicise a nest.

before.name: Sumatran palm civet
before.habitat: Woodland, gardens and some urban areas
before.rarity: Widespread but mostly hidden by day
before.fact: Seeds from fruit meals can be spread in a civet’s droppings.
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.summary: A nocturnal fruit-eater and small-animal hunter, often known locally as the common palm civet. It can move through both trees and settled areas in search of food.
before.identification: A long body and tail, pointed muzzle and dark facial markings. It is a civet, not a domestic cat despite the nickname ‘toddy cat’.
before.diet: Fruit, berries and small animals, including insects.
before.activity: Nocturnal; usually rests out of sight by day.
before.behaviour: Often forages alone, using branches and the ground. Adaptability allows it to visit gardens and buildings beside green spaces.
before.reproduction: Females give birth to dependent young in sheltered places. Avoid disturbing roof spaces or tree hollows occupied by a family.
before.singapore: A native resident of wooded areas and some neighbourhoods. The name Sumatran palm civet follows NParks’ current species table.
before.ecologicalRole: Passes seeds from eaten fruit, helping seed dispersal.
before.pressures: Road crossings, loss of shelter and conflict around homes. Wildlife-friendly coexistence is preferable to feeding or trapping.
before.watch: Secure food waste and allow it to leave. If young are present, seek AVS advice before closing an access hole.

before.name: White-bellied sea eagle
before.fact: Broad wings form a shallow V while it soars above waterways.
before.globalStatus: Least Concern · 2022
before.summary: A large coastal raptor often seen circling above Singapore’s water. Adult and young birds look quite different, so a brown eagle is not automatically another species.
before.identification: Adults have a white head and underside with grey upperparts. Young birds are mottled brown. Broad wings are held in a shallow V when soaring.
before.diet: Fish and other animals taken around waterways; also scavenges.
before.activity: Diurnal, often soaring above water.
before.behaviour: Uses rising air to soar while looking for food. Pairs build large stick nests in suitable tall trees.
before.reproduction: Both adults help with nesting and care for chicks. Nests may be reused and enlarged over successive years.
before.singapore: Occurs around reservoirs, rivers and the coast. It can be observed from many public waterfronts without approaching a nest.
before.ecologicalRole: A high-level predator and scavenger associated with aquatic food webs.
before.pressures: Protecting large nesting trees and limiting disturbance helps keep suitable habitat available.
before.watch: Use binoculars from a safe viewpoint. Never fly a drone near a nest or move closer to force a take-off.

funFacts.text: Brown juvenile plumage changes gradually into the adult white-and-grey pattern.

before.name: Wild boar
before.habitat: Forest, scrub and adjoining green spaces
before.rarity: Regular in suitable habitat; varies by site
before.fact: Piglets have pale stripes that become less obvious as they grow.
before.globalStatus: Dated assessment not verified in this edition
before.summary: One of Singapore’s largest land mammals. Its strong snout turns leaf litter and soil while it searches for food, so disturbed ground can be a clue to its presence.
before.identification: A stocky body with coarse dark hair, an elongated snout and short legs. Young piglets have pale lengthwise stripes that fade with age.
before.diet: Roots, fruit and other plant parts, plus invertebrates and carrion.
before.activity: Can be active by day or night; timing changes with disturbance.
before.behaviour: Roots through the ground for food. Females may travel with young; an animal with piglets or no escape route needs particular space.
before.reproduction: Females give birth to litters and nurse their piglets. Young follow their mother after an early period in shelter.
before.singapore: Occurs in forests and adjoining green areas, and may enter urban spaces. Encounter frequency varies greatly between places.
before.ecologicalRole: An omnivore whose rooting changes soil and leaf litter.
before.pressures: Human food, roads and encounters near urban edges can lead to conflict. Never encourage it to approach people.
before.watch: Stay calm, keep your distance and avoid separating adults from piglets. Do not feed or corner a boar.
